title: Does the Readout Bypass Leak the Input? A Feature-Visibility Audit of Hybrid Quantum-Classical Models
authors: Guilin Zhang, Kai Zhao, Xiquan Cui, Henry Heng, Xu Chu, Aletta Johanna Blanken
abstract: Readout-side residual hybrids concatenate raw inputs with measured quantum features. Under single-example gradient sharing, a biased first linear layer admits standard analytic recovery of its input, so the bypass exposes raw coordinates without requiring inversion of the quantum circuit. We audit this mechanism using two tabular datasets, four architectures, and metrics conditioned on feature visibility. Iterative gradient matching gives median full-record PSNR of 73-96 dB for residual and input-only heads. Quantum-only heads score 8-11 dB on the full record but 54-96 dB on the six input coordinates they actually encode. These are reconstruction results for the tested six-input, six-observable circuits, not a general statement about quantum encodings. A loss-threshold membership attack remains near chance. The contribution is a visibility-conditioned privacy audit: omitted coordinates must not be credited as protection supplied by quantum processing, and near-exact PSNR differences must not be interpreted as meaningful privacy rankings. Our findings concern individual gradients and do not establish leakage under aggregation or multiple local training steps.
summary: This work provides a privacy audit for hybrid quantum-classical models, demonstrating that the readout mechanism leaks raw input data through standard linear layer vulnerabilities. The authors show that simply appending quantum features does not guarantee privacy protection against gradient-based reconstruction attacks. This highlights that the leakage stems from the classical readout structure rather than the quantum processing itself.
main_problem: The paper audits the privacy leakage when raw classical inputs are concatenated with measured quantum features in readout-side residual hybrid Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models.
main_result: The readout bypass mechanism leaks raw input coordinates because the initial linear layer is analytically vulnerable, regardless of the quantum circuit's complexity.
method: The authors use gradient matching attacks and reconstruction metrics (PSNR, MSE) to quantify how well raw inputs can be recovered from the model's gradients.
model_or_system: The model is a readout-side residual hybrid QML architecture where the readout vector $z$ is formed by concatenating raw input $x$ and measured quantum features $Q(x)$.
key_observables: PSNR (Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio) for reconstruction, Membership Inference Attack (MIA) AUC, and reconstruction fidelity across full-vector vs. shared-six coordinates.
important_parameters: The analysis is limited to specific six-input, six-observable circuits and individual gradient leakage, not aggregation.
main_assumptions: The findings are specific to the tested small datasets and circuit structures, and the leakage is attributed to the linear layer's analytic vulnerability.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the visibility-conditioned audit setup, comparing reconstruction performance across different feature sets and architectures.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the model setup, details the gradient matching attack methodology, presents quantitative results comparing different architectural leakage levels (Residual vs. Input-only), and concludes with a privacy audit framework.
why_interesting: While focused on ML privacy, the underlying concept of analyzing information leakage through complex, non-linear quantum feature maps relates to understanding the information capacity and robustness of quantum representations.
